arc_intro:
FQ-171 — Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

Last piece of compute: we've been paying On-Demand for everything, and I don't think that's right for all of it. Some of this fleet is stable and predictable, some is bursty, and if we ever run real batch or ML workloads, some of it should be interruptible-and-cheap instead of always-on-and-expensive. Let's actually match pricing model to workload.

And — it's time. We understand this account much better now than we did six weeks ago. Let's finally figure out what i-0a9b8c7d6e5f4a3b2 actually is.

— Ravi
arc_outro:
Ravi Krishnan — FQ-171 update:

So that's what it was. A migration script, run once successfully, left running because the person who ran it left two weeks later and nobody else knew it existed. Same shape as Vikram back in FQ-142, just compute instead of access. I don't think that's a coincidence — I think it's literally what 'nobody owned this full-time for two years' actually looked like, twice.

Reserved pricing is in place where it makes sense, Spot is set up for the ML batch work, and that instance is finally gone — roughly ₹10.4 lakh spent on nothing, over 18 months, closed out for good.

That's compute done. Storage's next, and the CFO's office is asking questions directly this time — that alone should tell you something about where this is going.

— Ravi

tasks.question: Before deciding what to change, what's the most useful first question to ask about each workload?
options: A) Which instances are the biggest, since bigger instances always benefit most from any pricing change

B) How STABLE and PREDICTABLE is this workload's runtime pattern — does it run continuously long-term, does it vary, or is it a short, interruptible, one-off task? Pricing model choice depends entirely on this, not on instance size
C) Which instances were launched most recently, since only newer instances are eligible for pricing changes
D) Nothing needs to be asked — On-Demand is always the correct default for every workload

tasks.question: At a high level, what are the three main EC2 pricing models, and what's each one's basic trade-off?
options: A) On-Demand, Reserved, and Spot are just three different names AWS uses for the exact same pricing, chosen randomly per account

B) On-Demand: pay per hour/second with zero commitment, most flexible but most expensive. Reserved: commit to 1 or 3 years for a significant discount (roughly 40-60% off On-Demand), best for stable long-term workloads. Spot: use spare AWS capacity at a steep discount (70-90% off), but AWS can reclaim it with short notice — best for interruption-tolerant workloads
C) Reserved Instances can be cancelled at any time with no penalty, making the 1/3-year commitment purely optional
D) Spot instances are always more expensive than On-Demand, but guarantee they'll never be interrupted
tasks.explanation: Moonu different different trade-off — On-Demand flexible but expensive, Reserved for commitment instead of real discount (40-60%), Spot steepest discount (70-90%) but interruption risk is there. Ovvoruthukum different different fit-but workload is there.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — flexibility vs discount vs interruption-risk, moonume vera vera trade-off.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — moonume different trade-offs. Reserved commitment real-a is there, Spot cheapest but interruptible.

tasks.question: A workload has been running steadily for over a year with no planned changes, and is expected to keep running the same way for the foreseeable future. What's the main risk of NOT moving it from On-Demand to Reserved pricing?
options: A) There's no real risk — On-Demand and Reserved cost exactly the same for stable, long-running workloads

B) Continuing to pay On-Demand rates for a genuinely stable, long-running workload means paying significantly more (often 40-60% more) than necessary, month after month, for a commitment risk that's actually very low given the workload's proven stability
C) On-Demand pricing automatically converts to Reserved pricing after 12 months with no action needed
D) Reserved Instances are riskier than On-Demand for stable workloads, since they lock in a potentially outdated instance type

tasks.scenario: karthik-dev asks: 'If we Reserve order-service's baseline 3 instances, and the ASG later terminates one of them and launches a replacement during a scale-in/scale-out cycle, do we lose the Reserved discount?'
tasks.question: How should you answer?
options: A) Yes — Reserved Instance discounts are tied to one specific, permanent instance ID and are lost the moment that exact instance is terminated

B) No — a Reserved Instance's discount applies automatically to ANY running instance matching its attributes (instance type, region, platform), not to one specific instance ID. As long as at least 3 matching instances are running at any time, the discount applies to 3 of them, regardless of which specific instances they are
C) No, but only if the replacement instance is manually re-registered with AWS Support
D) Reserved Instances can only be used with instances that never get replaced under any circumstances, making them incompatible with ASGs entirely

tasks.ren_correct: Correct — attribute-based application, specific instance for ID tied not. ASG's compatible.

tasks.scenario: For the new overnight ML recommendation-model training job, ananya-analyst asks: 'What happens to the training progress if AWS actually does reclaim the Spot instance mid-run?'
tasks.question: How should this actually be handled, given Spot instances can be interrupted?
options: A) Nothing can be done — if a Spot instance is interrupted, all training progress is always lost completely and permanently

B) The training job should periodically checkpoint its progress (save state to durable storage like S3 or EBS at regular intervals), so if interrupted, a new Spot instance can resume from the last checkpoint instead of starting over from scratch — this is exactly the pattern that makes Spot viable for this kind of workload
C) Spot instances should never be used for ML training under any circumstances, regardless of checkpointing
D) Interruptions only happen if the instance has been running for over 24 hours, so short training runs are automatically safe without checkpointing

tasks.diagnosis: The instance was a one-time database migration helper, created by rohan.d (a contractor/engineer no longer with the company) roughly 18 months ago, to migrate the orders table to a new schema ahead of FoodQuick's Series A. The migration completed successfully and was verified — rohan.d's own README explicitly says to terminate the instance afterward. But rohan.d left the company approximately two weeks later, and with no dedicated infrastructure owner at the time (per the same 'nobody owned this full-time for two years' pattern behind everything else in this ticket), the termination step was simply never done. It sat running, doing nothing, for 18 months.
tasks.fix: Since the investigation confirms exactly what the instance was for, that its job completed successfully long ago, and that its own creator explicitly documented it should be terminated — take one final snapshot for the record (in case anything is ever questioned later), then terminate the instance for good.

cases.case_3: A brand-new experimental feature the team isn't sure will be kept past the next month

correct_answers.case_1: Reserved (1 or 3-year) — guaranteed capacity and predictability matter most here; Spot's interruption risk is unacceptable for payment processing
correct_answers.case_2: Spot with checkpointing — interruption-tolerant, cost savings matter more than guaranteed uptime for a batch job that can resume
correct_answers.case_3: On-Demand — committing to a 1-year Reserved Instance for something that might not exist next month is exactly the wrong trade-off; flexibility matters more here than discount
correct_answers.case_4: Reserved — the baseline is essentially always running by definition, making it a strong candidate for the commitment discount, same reasoning as reporting-db-01/notification-worker
